source.title: MoE-LPR: Multilingual Extension of Large Language Models through Mixture-of-Experts with Language Priors Routing
source.authors: Hao Zhou; Zhijun Wang; Shujian Huang; Xin Huang; Xue Han; Jun-Lan Feng; Chao Deng; Wei-Hua Luo; Jia-Jun Chen

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports downstream benchmark scores across model-size configurations, bearing on V6, but does not measure held-out loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The scaling experiments report average downstream benchmark scores in Table 7. They do not report held-out cross-entropy loss, power-law fits, extrapolation from smaller runs, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Other benchmark results compare training methods rather than isolate a scaling relation and are not included as scaling rows.
record.test_reason: This is a multilingual post-pretraining method paper. Its 'Scaling Law' section compares downstream benchmark averages of the authors' own method (MoE-LPR, by expert count) against two baselines (LLaMA-Pro by added layers, LoRAMoE by rank). All runs are continued training of one 1.8B base model on a fixed 24B tokens. There is no held-out loss, no power-law fit, no extrapolation, no compute allocation, and no test of whether downstream scores follow scale or loss predictably. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as motivation for adding parameters. The results are method-scalability comparisons, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that MoE-LPR scales better than LLaMA-Pro and LoRAMoE. Its expanded-language scores rise with more experts while original-language forgetting stays stable, and inference cost per token is unchanged. Their 'Scaling Law' section is a method-scalability comparison; they fit no law of any kind.
record.recipe_differences: Multilingual post-pretraining and downstream benchmark sweeps over expert counts, added layers, and LoRA ranks; no held-out-loss scaling-law fit, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream averages vary with architecture/configuration: LLaMA-Pro layer count, LoRAMoE rank, MoE-LPR expert count, and whether results are for expanded or original languages.

fits_no_version.finding: In expanded-language continued pretraining of Qwen1.5-1.8B, the gains from added parameters depend on the expansion method. MoE-LPR rises only from 44.05 to 45.41 as total parameters go from 2.6B to 7.4B, with active parameters fixed. LLaMA-Pro is non-monotonic (40.47, 41.10, 40.07), and its original-language score falls as layers are added.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream gains from adding parameters during continued pretraining depend on how the parameters are added, and saturate quickly when total but not active parameters grow.

record.problems: The scaling evidence is downstream benchmark averages rather than held-out loss; the comparison varies architecture and training method as well as parameter count, so size effects are not isolated. Results concern one base model and three expanded plus three original languages. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No Table 7 scaling rows left out.

untested.parts: No fixed-parameter shape comparison on loss.
No power-law fit in post-pretraining or any other regime.
There is no test of predictable downstream improvement with scale or loss. The configurations differ by method and are confounded with training.

record.verdict_notes: Despite the section titled 'Scaling Law', every row compares post-pretraining methods or configurations against an untrained base model. The reader's 'reversed' states for original languages conflate catastrophic forgetting with scaling. I relabelled all rows to none, and gave no verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their growth with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count and their effect on loss.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures downstream benchmark performance across configurations, but does not test predictive fits, relate downstream scores to pretraining loss, or establish a general scaling law.
Sensitivity of fitted loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations to setup or fitting choices.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: MoE-LPR expanded-language benchmark averages across expert counts
reader_labels.reason: The scores are substantially above the base reference and generally higher for larger expert configurations, though not strictly monotonic; see R6-R9.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Original-language averages and non-MoE-LPR size/configuration comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Original-language scores are below the base-model reference, and LLaMA-Pro expanded-language scores are non-monotonic across layer counts; see R1-R5 and R10-R19.
